text: Given an integer n, break it into a sum of at least two positive integers and maximize their product. Return that maximum product.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — I must split into at least two parts, so n itself isn't allowed as one piece, each part is a positive integer, and I want the max product?
Right. n is up to fifty-eight.

Let me run through an example. Ten splits as three plus three plus four, which gives three times three times four, thirty-six. That beats five plus five, which gives twenty-five, or five twos, which give thirty-two. So the answer is thirty-six.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would try every way to write n as a sum, and the number of those grows exponentially. This problem reminds me of rod cutting: a DP over where to make a cut. Let dp of i be the max product of breaking i into at least two parts. At each cut point j, the other piece, i minus j, has two options: leave it whole, giving j times i minus j, or break it further, giving j times dp of i minus j. Take the max of both.

Here's the plan. One: build dp from two up to n. Two: for each i, try every cut point j from one to i minus one. Three: keep the max of j times i minus j and j times dp of i minus j, then return dp of n. One thing worth flagging — both terms are needed because dp of i minus j is defined as must break, so it excludes leaving i minus j whole. That whole case is exactly the j times i minus j term. Concretely, dp of two is one and dp of three is two here, not two and three. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Good. Code the DP, and mention the math shortcut if you know it.

The DP starts every entry at one and runs the double loop; the inner line takes the max of the cut term and the no-cut term. And a linear-time math version — the optimal split favors threes. It returns one and two for n of two and three, then peels off threes while n is above four, and multiplies in the leftover. Both give the same answer. One thing worth flagging — for the math version, a leftover one is wasteful, since it only multiplies by one. So I fold three plus one into four, which is two times two; the while n greater than four bound handles that at the end.

Let's dry-run the DP and highlight cut versus no cut. The row that matters is eight with a cut at three. Keeping five whole gives fifteen, but breaking it gives three times dp of five, which is three times six, eighteen. So the cut wins and dp of eight is eighteen. Small pieces like two and three stay whole; big ones, five and up, get broken. Ten gives thirty-six. That matches. Corner cases: two gives one, three gives two, and four gives four. At fifty-eight, the answer still fits in an int.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is n squared for the DP and linear for the math version; space is linear and constant. Oh, one more thing — the key subtlety is the two terms: dp of i minus j forces a break, so the keep-it-whole case must be added as j times i minus j. And the reason threes win is that the cube root of three beats the square root of two — three has the best per-unit product. For a huge n, I'd compute three to the n over three with fast exponentiation, in log n time.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You explained why both DP terms exist — the must-break definition needs the whole-piece term — and that dp of two is one, not two. You showed cut versus no cut concretely. And you gave the split-into-threes math, with the reasoning and the log n extension. Good work.
